articles.title: What is a glob?
articles.summary: A compact way to describe sets of paths using wildcards

blocks.content: A glob is a template that either matches a path or doesn't. It's not code that executes, nor a regular expression: it's a matching pattern. The name comes from a Unix program called glob — short for global — meant to expand wildcards on the command line.
This is what determines whether a rule fires or not when Claude works with a file.
The pattern `src/**/*.ts` matches:

articles.title: Single asterisk: *
articles.summary: Any string within one path segment (doesn't cross directories)

blocks.content: `*` matches any string of characters within a single path segment. **The key nuance: it doesn't cross directory separators** (`/`).

blocks.label: Pattern: src/*.ts
blocks.content:
✓ src/index.ts
✓ src/utils.ts
✗ src/utils/helpers.ts    (there's another level in between)
✗ index.ts                (not inside src/)
Other examples:
`**` matches any string **including directory separators**. It crosses as many levels as needed. The difference from `*` is fundamental.

items.title: src/**/*.ts
items.body: .ts files in src/ and in any of its subdirectories

blocks.content: **At the start: 'anywhere in the project'**

blocks.label: Examples
blocks.content:
**/node_modules    — any node_modules, regardless of location
**/*.log            — all logs
**/src              — every folder named src
**In the middle: skips unknown levels**

blocks.label: Examples
blocks.content:
src/**/*.test.ts       — tests in src, at any depth
packages/**/dist       — the dist folder of any package
src/**/config/db.ts    — db.ts inside any config folder in src
**At the end: 'everything from here on'**

blocks.label: Examples
blocks.content:
docs/**              — absolutely everything inside docs
src/legacy/**        — the entire contents of the legacy directory
`**` must appear as a **complete segment** between slashes. `src**/foo` doesn't work as a globstar; the correct form is `src/**/foo`.
If you want three specific subdirectories out of six that exist, use brace expansion instead of `**`:

blocks.label: Example
blocks.content:
src/directory/{alpha,beta,gamma}/**/*.java

Matches: src/directory/alpha/Model.java
         src/directory/beta/sub/Repo.java
         src/directory/gamma/Service.java

Doesn't match: src/directory/delta/Config.java
`?` matches **exactly one** character of any kind, except the `/` separator. Much more restrictive than `*`: used when you know the exact length of what you're looking for.

blocks.label: Pattern: test?.js
blocks.content:
✓ test1.js        (one character)
✓ testA.js        (one character)
✗ test.js         (missing a character)
✗ test10.js       (that's two characters)

blocks.label: Pattern: v?.?.?.md
blocks.content:
✓ v1.2.3.md       (short version)
✓ v9.0.1.md       (short version)
✗ v1.10.0.md      ('10' is two characters)
Used sparingly in practice, but useful for fixed-format names: short version numbers, identifiers with a strict length.

articles.title: Character classes: [ ]
articles.summary: A single character from a set

blocks.content: Brackets let you specify a set of acceptable characters for a single position. It matches exactly one of the listed characters.

blocks.label: Patterns
blocks.content:
log-[0-9].txt      — log-0.txt through log-9.txt
v[0-9].[0-9].ts    — v1.0.ts, v2.3.ts...
[A-Z]*.md          — .md files starting with an uppercase letter
If the first character inside the brackets is `!`, the meaning is inverted: it matches any character that is **not** in the set.

blocks.label: Examples
blocks.content:
[!0-9]*.txt      — .txt whose name does NOT start with a digit
[!_]*.js         — .js whose name does NOT start with an underscore
**Note:** negation inside brackets `[!abc]` only affects that single position in the pattern. To exclude entire paths you use `!pattern` at the start of a line — a different mechanism.
Braces let you list comma-separated alternatives. The pattern matches if the path matches **any** of them. Especially useful for grouping extensions.

items.title: {src,lib,packages}/**/*.ts
items.body: TS in any of the three dirs

blocks.label: Complex pattern
blocks.content:
src/directory/{alpha,beta,gamma}/**/*.java

✓ src/directory/alpha/Model.java
✓ src/directory/beta/sub/Repo.java
✓ src/directory/gamma/Service.java
✗ src/directory/delta/Config.java
✗ src/directory/epsilon/Utils.java
Alternatives can contain full path segments. This is exactly what lets you select three specific subdirectories without repeating the whole pattern.
A pattern starting with `!` excludes paths from the accumulated set. They're evaluated in order: first you include a broad set, then you trim what you don't want.

subsections.title: Example 1: All TS without tests or generated code

blocks.label: Patterns
blocks.content:
**/*.ts                    — include all TS
!**/*.test.ts              — except tests
!**/*.spec.ts              — and specs
!**/node_modules/**        — and never anything from node_modules
!src/**/generated/**        — nor generated code

blocks.label: Patterns
blocks.content:
docs/**/*.md               — include markdown docs
!docs/**/DRAFT-*.md        — except drafts
Don't confuse `[!abc]` (character negation at one position) with `!pattern` (whole-pattern negation). They are **completely different** mechanisms.
The classic mistake: writing `src/*.ts` expecting it to cover all of src, and being surprised that files in subdirectories don't show up.
**Mental rule:** a single asterisk doesn't cross slashes, two do. As soon as a pattern 'isn't picking up what's inside folders,' swap `*` for `**/*`.
Writing `src**` or `**foo` doesn't work as a globstar in most implementations. The globstar wants to live alone between separators: `src/**/foo`, not `src**/foo`.

They aren't. In a glob, the dot `.` is a literal dot, not 'any character.' `app.js` in a glob means exactly `app.js`. And there are no quantifiers like `+` or `{3,5}`: if you need that, globs aren't the tool.

Files starting with a dot (`.env`, `.gitignore`) are often outside what a generic pattern captures. A `*.json` may not catch `.babelrc.json` depending on the implementation. If you want to include them, be explicit: `.*` or `**/.*.json`.

rows: Any string within one segment. Doesn't cross slashes.
Any string crossing directories. Must be isolated between slashes.
Exactly one character. Doesn't cross slashes.
One character from the set or range.
A character NOT in the set.
Excludes paths matching the pattern. Goes at the start.
Literal dot. In globs it doesn't mean 'any character.'

articles.title: Tips for writing globs
articles.summary: A strategy for writing correct patterns

items.title: Which exact files should trigger the rule?
items.body: Be specific. For example: 'all TypeScript tests in src'

items.title: Which similar files should be left out?
items.body: Think about files that look alike but you don't want: .test.js vs .test.ts, /src vs /dist

items.title: Are there any trap subdirectories?
items.body: node_modules, dist, build — worth excluding explicitly

blocks.content: Answering those three questions first makes the pattern write almost itself.
